title: Given an m by n board of characters and a list of words, return all words that can be formed by sequentially adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically neighboring), where each cell is used at most once per word.
shortTitle: Word Search II — Trie + DFS backtracking on grid

s1_definition.profdef: Word Search II builds a Trie from the dictionary of words, then runs a single depth-first backtracking search over the grid, advancing a Trie pointer as it moves between adjacent cells. When the pointer reaches a node marked as a word end, that word is collected. The Trie prunes the search by stopping any path whose prefix is not shared by any dictionary word.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a grid of letters printed on a fraud-detection heat map and a watchlist of suspicious code words. Instead of hunting for each watchlist word separately, you build one big index of all the words and sweep the grid once. At each cell you check the index: if the letters you have walked so far are not the start of any watchlist word, you abandon that path immediately. When a walked path completes a watchlist word, you record a hit.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put all dictionary words in one Trie, DFS the grid with backtracking while walking the Trie, collect words at end-of-word nodes, and prune paths whose prefix no word shares.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Search II builds a Trie from the dictionary of words, then runs a single depth-first backtracking search over the grid, advancing a Trie pointer as it moves between adjacent cells. When the pointer reaches a node marked as a word end, that word is collected. The Trie prunes the search by stopping any path whose prefix is not shared by any dictionary word.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a grid of letters printed on a fraud-detection heat map and a watchlist of suspicious code words. Instead of hunting for each watchlist word separately, you build one big index of all the words and sweep the grid once. At each cell you check the index: if the letters you have walked so far are not the start of any watchlist word, you abandon that path immediately. When a walked path completes a watchlist word, you record a hit.

**One line to remember:** Put all dictionary words in one Trie, DFS the grid with backtracking while walking the Trie, collect words at end-of-word nodes, and prune paths whose prefix no word shares.

sections.s2_technical:
First build a Trie from all the words so that prefixes are shared and the search can test many words at once. It helps to store the complete word string on the end-of-word node so collection is immediate. For example: `node.word = word;` at the end of each insert.

Then run a depth-first search starting from every cell. The search carries the current Trie node; before entering a cell, it checks whether the cell's character is a child of the current Trie node, and if not it returns at once, which is the pruning step. For example: `TrieNode next = node.children.get(board[r][c]); if (next == null) return;`.

When the search reaches a node whose word field is set, it adds that word to the result set and clears the field to avoid duplicates. It then marks the current cell as visited, recurses into the four neighbors, and on return restores the cell so other paths can reuse it. For example: mark `board[r][c] = '#';` recurse, then `board[r][c] = original;` to backtrack.

The time cost in the worst case is the number of cells times four to the power of the maximum word length, but the Trie pruning cuts this dramatically in practice because dead prefixes are abandoned early. A senior nuance is sharing one Trie across all words so the grid is swept once rather than once per word, storing the word on the terminal node for O(1) collection, and optionally pruning leaf Trie nodes after a word is found to shrink the tree as the search proceeds.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a transaction-pattern grid encodes flagged activity as a matrix of characters, and the compliance team maintains a watchlist of coded patterns. The system must find every watchlist pattern that appears as a connected path of adjacent cells in the grid. This is exactly how Word Search II works — it discovers all dictionary words embedded as adjacent-cell paths.

Problem 2 — The watchlist can hold many patterns, so searching the grid separately for each would be wasteful. This is exactly why a single shared Trie plus one grid sweep with pruning is used.

The mini-project builds a `PatternGridSearch` service that constructs a Trie from the watchlist and returns all matched patterns, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a four-by-four grid and a watchlist of four patterns.

Step 1: The service builds one Trie holding FRAUD, RISK, AUD, and SAFE, with each terminal node storing its full word.

Step 2: The sweep starts at cell zero-zero, the letter F. The Trie has an F child, so the search continues, walking R, A, U, D along adjacent cells and reaching the terminal node for FRAUD, which is collected and its word field cleared.

Step 3: From the cell holding A inside the grid, the search walks A, U, D and reaches the AUD terminal node, collecting AUD.

Step 4: Starting at the R in the third row, the search walks R, I, S, K and reaches the RISK terminal, collecting RISK.

Step 5: For SAFE, the search tries to begin at any S cell, but the required adjacent continuation A then F then E does not exist as a connected path, so the Trie prunes the path and SAFE is never collected.

Step 6: Every other starting cell whose character is not a child of the Trie root is pruned immediately, so the sweep stays cheap. The final result holds FRAUD, AUD, and RISK.

```text
2026-10-26T20:30:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Fraud Pattern Grid Search
2026-10-26T20:30:00Z [INFO] Patterns matched in grid: [FRAUD, AUD, RISK]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Grid:            Trie (watchlist):
  F R A U            root─F─R─A─U─D●
  X A U D                 ├─R─I─S─K●
  R I S K                 ├─A─U─D●
  Y K E D                 └─S─A─F─E●

  DFS from each cell, walk Trie in lock-step:
    F(0,0)→R→A→U→D ⇒ FRAUD ●  collected
    A(1,1)→U→D     ⇒ AUD   ●  collected
    R(2,0)→I→S→K   ⇒ RISK  ●  collected
    S cells → no adjacent A-F-E path → pruned (SAFE not found)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search II asks for every dictionary word that can be traced through adjacent cells of a grid, each cell used at most once per word. The naive approach runs a separate grid search for each word, which repeats enormous amounts of work. My efficient solution builds one Trie from all the words so their shared prefixes are tested together, then sweeps the grid a single time with a depth-first backtracking search that walks a Trie pointer in lock-step with the grid path.

Before stepping into a cell, I check whether its character is a child of the current Trie node, and if not I abandon the path immediately. This pruning is the whole reason the single-Trie approach wins: any prefix that no dictionary word shares is cut off at once. When the Trie pointer reaches a node whose stored word field is set, I collect that word and clear the field so the same word is not reported twice. I mark the cell visited before recursing into its four neighbors and restore it on the way back so other paths can reuse it, which is the backtracking.

The details interviewers look for are sharing one Trie across all words rather than one per word, storing the full word string on the terminal node for constant-time collection, and the correct mark-and-restore to enforce the use-each-cell-once rule per path. The worst-case cost is the number of cells times four to the power of the longest word length, but pruning makes the practical cost far smaller.

In my project at National Bank of India, I applied this to a fraud-pattern grid where flagged activity is encoded as a character matrix and compliance keeps a watchlist of coded patterns. Building one Trie from the whole watchlist let me find every embedded pattern in a single sweep, and the prefix pruning meant dead starting cells were discarded instantly rather than driving a full search per watchlist entry.
